subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 34-year-old laboratory technician in a biodefense research facility develops fever, a painless black necrotic ulcer on the forearm, and profound nonpitting edema of the surrounding tissue with painless regional lymphadenopathy. Two days later he has dyspnea, widened mediastinum on chest radiograph, and pleural effusions. He works with spore-forming gram-positive rods cultured from soil samples.
question: Which of the following is the most likely agent, and which feature most supports it?

options.text: Yersinia pestis; the buboes and hemoptysis of pneumonic plague
Francisella tularensis; the tick bite and ulceroglandular tularemia
Brucella species; the undulant fever with sacroiliitis
Clostridium botulinum; the symmetric descending flaccid paralysis
B anthracis; painless eschar and a widened mediastinum

explanation_correct: Cutaneous anthrax from Bacillus anthracis begins as a painless papule that ulcerates into a black eschar with marked edema, and inhalation anthrax produces a widened mediastinum with hemorrhagic mediastinitis after spores are inhaled. B anthracis is a spore-forming gram-positive rod and is one of the classic bioterrorism agents because of its ability to be aerosolized as spores. Its anthrax toxin acts by mimicking adenylate cyclase.

explanation_incorrect.A: Y pestis causes bubonic plague with painful buboes and pneumonic plague with hemoptysis; it does not produce a black eschar with a widened mediastinum.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tularemia from F tularensis produces an ulceroglandular illness after tick or rabbit exposure without a black eschar or mediastinal widening.
explanation_incorrect.C: Brucellosis produces undulant fever with sacroiliitis after unpasteurized dairy exposure rather than eschar and mediastinal hemorrhage.
explanation_incorrect.D: Botulism produces symmetric descending flaccid paralysis from a neurotoxin, not a cutaneous eschar or a mediastinal mass.

educationalObjective: Bacillus anthracis is a spore-forming gram-positive rod and bioterrorism agent; cutaneous anthrax produces a painless black eschar and inhalation anthrax a widened mediastinum.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 45-year-old man from a rural area of New Mexico presents with 6 days of fever, chills, and a painful left inguinal lymph node the size of a golf ball. He notes that a prairie dog near his cabin died of a similar wasting illness and that he was bitten by fleas while camping. He has a productive cough with blood-streaked sputum, and Gram stain shows bipolar-staining gram-negative rods.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Yersinia pestis causes plague and is transmitted by fleas, with rats and prairie dogs serving as reservoirs. Bipolar-staining gram-negative rods with a safety-pin appearance are the classic morphology, and the painful enlarged node is a bubo; progression to pneumonic plague causes hemoptysis. Plague is one of the classic bioterrorism agents.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anthrax causes a painless black eschar and mediastinal widening, and B anthracis is a large spore-forming gram-positive rod rather than a gram-negative rod.
explanation_incorrect.B: Brucellosis produces undulant fever with back pain after unpasteurized dairy consumption and does not give buboes or pneumonic spread.
explanation_incorrect.C: RMSF from R rickettsii is tick-borne and produces a rash spreading from the wrists and ankles to the trunk with headache and fever, not suppurating buboes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tularemia from F tularensis follows tick, rabbit, or deer-fly exposure and produces ulceroglandular disease, not the flea-prairie dog reservoir pattern with bipolar rods of plague.

educationalObjective: Yersinia pestis is flea-borne with rodent reservoirs, shows bipolar-staining gram-negative rods, and causes bubonic plague that can progress to pneumonic plague.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 38-year-old veterinarian who assists with sheep and cattle births in a rural county develops a 2-week history of high fever, severe retro-orbital headache, dry cough, and right upper quadrant tenderness. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated. Several farmers in the region had similar febrile illnesses after assisting with lambing, and one reported that the amniotic fluid may have aerosolized in the barn.
question: Which organism is the most likely cause of this cluster of illness?
explanation_correct: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever and is transmitted by aerosols of cattle or sheep amniotic fluid, making obstetric work with livestock the classic exposure, and it produces fever, severe headache, and an atypical pneumonia with hepatitis-like liver enzyme elevation. The organism is an obligate intracellular bacterium and is highly infectious by the aerosol route, which matters for laboratory and biodefense handling. Brucella, also a livestock zoonosis, is instead acquired from unpasteurized dairy or direct tissue contact and gives undulant fever.

explanation_incorrect.B: C psittaci causes psittacosis with pneumonia after exposure to parrots and other birds, not livestock parturition.
explanation_incorrect.C: Leptospirosis is acquired from animal urine in water and produces fever, myalgias, and jaundice, not an amniotic-fluid aerosol outbreak.
explanation_incorrect.D: F tularensis is transmitted by ticks, rabbits, and deer flies and causes ulceroglandular tularemia, not an outbreak tied to lambing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Brucellosis produces undulant fever with sacroiliitis and back pain after unpasteurized dairy or direct tissue contact; it is not the organism specifically associated with amniotic fluid aerosols.

educationalObjective: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever via aerosols of cattle or sheep amniotic fluid and presents with high fever, headache, atypical pneumonia, and hepatitis.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 52-year-old dairy farmer presents with 3 weeks of undulant fever, drenching night sweats, low back pain, and weight loss. He drinks unpasteurized milk from his herd and has helped deliver calves bare-handed. MRI of the spine shows inflammation at the L4-L5 level. Blood cultures are persistently negative on routine media but eventually grow a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation_correct: Brucella causes brucellosis (undulant fever) and is acquired by ingestion of unpasteurized dairy or by inhalation of and contact with infected animal tissue or fluids, making dairy farmers and veterinarians the classic hosts. The classic complication is sacroiliitis and vertebral osteomyelitis with back pain, and the organism is a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus requiring prolonged culture. It is one of the zoonotic bacteria and one of the classic bioterrorism agents.

explanation_incorrect.A: Y pestis is flea-borne and produces buboes or pneumonic plague rather than undulant fever with sacroiliitis after milk ingestion.
explanation_incorrect.B: C burnetii causes Q fever through aerosolized amniotic fluid and produces pneumonia and hepatitis without the extensive vertebral osteomyelitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: M tuberculosis causes Pott disease, which also affects the spine, but it presents with a positive tuberculin test and acid-fast bacilli rather than a gram-negative coccobacillus after dairy exposure.
explanation_incorrect.E: S aureus is the most common cause of vertebral osteomyelitis overall, but it would grow promptly as coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci in clusters, and it does not explain the unpasteurized dairy exposure.

educationalObjective: Brucella causes undulant fever with sacroiliitis and vertebral osteomyelitis after unpasteurized dairy or animal tissue exposure and is a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 61-year-old man presents with 3 days of fever, headache, myalgias, and a rash that began on the wrists and ankles and now involves the trunk, palms, and soles. He recalls a tick bite after a hiking trip. Laboratory studies show hyponatremia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases. He is started on a tetracycline-class antibiotic empirically before the serology returns.
question: Which of the following statements best explains why this empiric choice is appropriate?

options.text: Rickettsia are extracellular gram-positive cocci, so a cell wall inhibitor such as vancomycin is required
Rickettsia are fungi, so ergosterol-binding polyenes should be used rather than antibacterials
Rickettsia lack ribosomes, so protein synthesis inhibitors have no activity and only fluoroquinolones work
Rickettsia are intracellular, so tetracyclines accumulate inside
Rickettsia are anaerobes, so metronidazole is the agent of choice

explanation_correct: Rocky Mountain spotted fever from Rickettsia rickettsii produces the classic triad of headache, fever, and rash, with the rash starting at the wrists and ankles and spreading to the trunk, palms, and soles. Rickettsia are obligate intracellular bacteria, and tetracyclines accumulate intracellularly, which is why doxycycline is the treatment for all rickettsial diseases, including RMSF. First Aid's palm-and-sole mnemonic groups RMSF with Coxsackievirus A hand-foot-mouth disease and secondary syphilis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Rickettsia are neither extracellular nor gram-positive cocci; they are obligate intracellular organisms, which is why a cell wall inhibitor such as vancomycin would fail against them.
explanation_incorrect.B: Rickettsia are bacteria with peptidoglycan-containing walls, not fungi, and treatment is with antibacterials such as doxycycline.
explanation_incorrect.C: Rickettsia have bacterial (70S) ribosomes and are susceptible to protein synthesis inhibitors including tetracyclines and chloramphenicol.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rickettsia are not treated with metronidazole, which is used for anaerobes and protozoa such as Trichomonas and Giardia.

educationalObjective: Rickettsia are obligate intracellular bacteria treated with doxycycline, which accumulates intracellularly; RMSF rash starts at wrists and ankles and spreads to palms and soles.
